description: Breaking Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2026.

talks.title: Wednesday
talks.teaser: Bundles talks on parser state bugs, exposed Airflow deployments, npm dependency confusion and open biohacking projects.
talks.summary:
This block bundles several Breaking Ground sessions. The opening talk argues that an input parser can correctly reject a file and still leave partial writes in live program state. The speaker demonstrates a loader that returns an error after already overwriting a function pointer, then surveys fifteen widely used C parsers and finds that most mutate caller-owned state before validation. The suggested fix is to parse into a staged copy and commit only after the full input has been validated.

A second talk looks at Apache Airflow deployments exposed on the internet. The speaker reports default administrator credentials, secrets kept in variables and DAG source, an unauthenticated Redis broker, a weak token signing check, and a connections API that masks sensitive fields by name rather than by value, exposing a Slack webhook. A third session describes a red-team exercise that published dependency-confusion packages to npm, which were later analysed and mistaken for a real supply chain campaign. The speaker discusses how public publishing leaks operational details and how such packages persist in caches and mirrors.

The remaining sessions cover an Argentine transport operator whose exposed systems were reached through a chain of small flaws, and a closing keynote about open, replicable pharmaceutical projects. The common thread is that small validation gaps, leaked credentials and careless public publishing create real exposure. The practical guidance includes staging writes, rotating exposed secrets, isolating brokers and consoles, pinning dependencies and tightening rules of engagement for red teams.

talks.title: Tuesday
talks.teaser: Bundles several offensive security talks on cloud abuse, network pivoting, kernel drivers, UEFI bootkits and Rust obfuscation.
talks.summary:
This recording is a multi-hour block of Breaking Ground talks rather than a single presentation. The opening session walks through compromising a hardened Active Directory estate by abusing CI/CD pipelines, runners and cloud identities, relying on built-in consoles and administrative functions instead of attack tools. It shows how a pipeline spanning data and control planes can become a route to domain-level impact.

Later sessions cover cloud shell services repurposed as hidden compute and storage, mapping network bridges and cross-protocol gateways in OT and out-of-band management devices, and analysing how pentesters actually chain commands across an engagement. Other talks look at bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver attacks against endpoint products, UEFI bootkit debugging and Secure Boot bypasses, a SIEM built on firewall log normalization, and an LLVM-based obfuscator for Rust binaries.

For practitioners, the common thread is that attackers exploit trusted features, identities and signed components rather than novel bugs. Useful takeaways include limiting the blast radius of credentials, treating CI/CD and cloud identity as control-plane assets, reducing standing privilege, disabling unused forwarding and out-of-band interfaces, and treating signed drivers and boot components as attack surface.

talks.title: Monday
talks.teaser: Recording of the Breaking Ground day covers cloud identity abuse, Go malware memory forensics, and business logic flaws.
talks.summary:
The recording runs through a full conference day in the Breaking Ground track. It opens with venue logistics, code of conduct reminders and a schedule overview before the technical sessions begin. Early talks cover attacker persistence in Google Cloud through workload identity federation, including open provider pools, silent edits to provider conditions, and rogue certificate trust anchors. They also explain the audit log gaps that hide this activity and offer queries and organization policies to catch it.

Middle sessions move into memory forensics for Go malware, where a set of Volatility 3 plugins recovers strings, function call graphs and active goroutines from memory samples. Other talks look at automated S/MIME certificate issuance over ACME, at dangling DNS records that point to released AWS Elastic IPs with a read-only detection script, and at email abuse through trusted cloud application workflows, device code phishing and multi-tenant authorization flaws. A business logic session shows how promo code guessing, refund abuse and order-edit gaps in e-commerce and ride-hailing apps can yield free goods and services.

Later sections include a policy keynote on how the Justice Department changed its stance toward good-faith security research, and a RISC-V talk on shadow stacks and landing pads for control-flow integrity. The practical takeaways across the day are to enable the right cloud logs, validate tokens and tenants on the server, monitor dangling DNS entries, and enforce business rules server side rather than trusting the client.
